author: blu
body: The registers have been driven all along -- but from inside the COMPILER, by X86_64Boot, which writes them as machine code during SMP bring-up and arms each core's timer. That is emit-time code: it builds instructions, it does not execute them, and nothing a guest program could call reached the LAPIC at all. `vga-terminal-demo` cited this chapter and called lapic-drain against a chapter that had never been written; the cite is now an error rather than a silence, which is how the gap was finally legible.

author: blu
body: The id sits in the top byte. codex-vm answers this per core, so an application processor and the boot processor give different answers -- which is the only reason it is worth reading.

author: blu
body: The version register is the honest liveness probe for this chapter. It is a fixed non-zero constant the hardware reports about itself, so a read that returns it proves the MMIO round trip reached a real decoder; a read that returns 0 is what a missing mapping, an unmapped BAR and a stub all return. Every other register here can read 0 legitimately.

author: blu
body: What codex-vm proves about this is nothing. Its LAPIC models the id, the version, the SIVR, the ICR and the per-core timer, and returns 0 for every other offset, the ISR included -- so under codex-vm the walk reads eight zero words, sends no EOI, and returns 0. That is a correct result on a machine with nothing in service, and it is indistinguishable from a driver that does not work. `codex/test/lapic-regs` therefore tests what the emulator can actually contradict and does not pretend the drain is covered.
